claims.text: The target material is bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen in a chemically disordered BCC high-entropy-alloy matrix.
Explicitly incorporating oxygen-defect configurations and local lattice distortions into DFT and coupling the results to Boltzmann transport will improve electrical-conductivity predictions.
The proposed calculations include electron–defect and electron–phonon scattering.
Electrical transport from nearly 0 to 200 K is dominated by quantum defect scattering and electron-coherence effects.
Electrical transport from 300 to 1200 K is dominated by phonon scattering, with additional contributions from oxygen-induced disorder.
Oxygen impurities induce local lattice distortions in the disordered BCC matrix.
Oxygen impurities create additional localized electron-scattering centers that are absent from perfect-crystal models.
At low temperatures, oxygen-related scattering centers and quantum-coherence effects produce non-monotonic or plateau-like conductivity.
At higher temperatures, phonon–defect scattering becomes pronounced.
Explicit treatment of these scattering mechanisms captures experimentally observed deviations from ideal-crystal predictions.
The proposed approach will predict lower electrical conductivity than perfect-crystal analytical models.
A held-out 300 K benchmark for a similar specimen is approximately 3.5 × 10^6 S/m.
The proposed method should predict the 300 K conductivity within ±10% of 3.5 × 10^6 S/m.
Traditional defect-free DFT models tend to overestimate conductivity because they neglect oxygen-defect and chemical-disorder scattering.
The proposed framework is applicable in the nearly 0–200 K and 300–1200 K ranges.
Outside the specified temperature ranges, the framework may not adequately capture the combined scattering mechanisms.
Statistical sampling of the many possible oxygen-defect configurations is a major source of uncertainty.
Accurately representing low-temperature quantum effects and high-temperature scattering rates is uncertain.
A 300 K prediction error greater than ±10% relative to the held-out benchmark would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe the expected low-temperature non-monotonic trend would falsify the hypothesis.
